Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that make me feel strong emotions
wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

issues.item: Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
issues.explanation: This item is the only maladaptive strategy that is hard to integrate with the rest of the profile. The threat items describe classic hypervigilant danger-monitoring (false alarms, waking to check safety, inability to relax), and the other strategy items reflect avoidance/concealment consistent with feeling unsafe. In contrast, deliberately seeking conflict or creating drama as a distraction points toward an externalizing/interpersonal regulation pattern that is not supported anywhere else in the selected triggers, memory, appraisal, or threat content. Given the formulation, Threat and Maladaptive Strategies should be tightly linked; this strategy does not plausibly arise from the specific threat pattern provided and makes the profile internally less coherent.

vignette:
Mariam was fifty years old, a divorced social worker who had built a quiet life in a Midwestern city after fleeing her home country more than a decade ago. The trauma she carried was not a single explosion or a moment of violence, but a slow, grinding year of threats, disappearances, and the final, desperate flight across a border with her two young children. She had left behind a brother who was never heard from again, and a house that was taken. In America, she found safety, but her body never seemed to believe it. She worked with refugee families now, helping them navigate housing and schools, and she was good at it—patient, knowledgeable. But the work itself was a constant exposure to stories that mirrored her own, and the emotional weight of those sessions would cling to her for days.

What Mariam noticed first, and what troubled her most, was how often she reacted as if she were in danger when nothing was actually wrong. A car backfiring outside her office window would send a jolt through her chest. A colleague touching her shoulder from behind could make her flinch and spin around, heart hammering. She would wake in the middle of the night, not from a nightmare but from a sudden, wordless alarm, and lie still in the dark, listening for footsteps that were never there. Even at home, with the door locked and the chain on, she could not truly relax. She would sit on her couch and find her eyes drifting to the window, scanning the street for anything unusual. This constant vigilance was exhausting, but it felt necessary—a kind of survival habit she could not shake.

Because Mariam had come to believe that being noticed was dangerous. She had learned this lesson in the most concrete way possible: people who stood out, who attracted attention, were the ones who disappeared. So she had developed a set of strategies to make herself invisible. She wore concealing clothing—loose, dark jackets and long skirts in muted colors—even in the summer heat. She avoided any situation that might stir strong emotions, because strong emotions drew eyes. She avoided crowded markets, public celebrations, even the waiting room at the clinic if it was too full. And she constantly scanned her environment, checking for exits, for faces that lingered too long, for anything that felt off. These were not choices she made consciously anymore; they were automatic, woven into the fabric of her days.

The harder she tried to stay hidden, the more her vigilance grew. Each time she scanned a room and found nothing, her relief was short-lived, because the scanning itself kept her locked in a state of alert. She would check her surroundings at the grocery store, then realize she had been so focused on watching that she had forgotten half her list. That failure—the feeling of being out of control—would make her scan even more carefully the next time. It was a cycle that tightened around her without her noticing. At work, she began to take her lunch break in her car rather than the staff room, because the staff room meant small talk and unpredictable questions. She told herself it was just more efficient. But her supervisor had started to comment that she seemed "on edge," and Mariam had deflected with a tight smile. She knew she was becoming isolated, but the alternative—letting her guard down—felt like an invitation to catastrophe.

What finally brought Mariam to seek help was a panic attack in the middle of a home visit. She was sitting at a kitchen table with a young mother from Syria, listening to her describe the night soldiers had come to her house, and Mariam felt the room tilt. Her vision narrowed, her chest locked, and she had to excuse herself to the bathroom, where she stood gripping the sink, telling herself she was not back there, she was here, she was safe. But the words meant nothing in that moment. Afterward, she could not stop thinking about how close she had come to falling apart in front of a client. She was afraid that next time, she would not be able to pull herself back. She was afraid that her own survival habits, which had once kept her alive, were now unraveling the life she had built. She wanted to learn how to feel safe without having to disappear.
